journeys.name: Diocletian's movements, 284-305
journeys.summary: Diocletian ruled from the road. Barnes' reconstruction of his itinerary from the dates and places of his laws shows an emperor who rarely stayed in one city for more than a season and visited Rome only once, for his twentieth anniversary. He was proclaimed by the eastern army near Nicomedia, beat Carinus on the Margus, and spent the next decade shuttling between the Danube, where he fought Sarmatians and Carpi, and Syria, where he fought Saracens and Persians, with a meeting in Milan to concert policy with Maximian. In 297-298 he crushed the Egyptian revolt of Domitius Domitianus after an eight-month siege of Alexandria and pulled the Nile frontier back to Philae. The Great Persecution was launched from Nicomedia in 303. After a miserable winter visit to Rome and a long illness he abdicated on 1 May 305 and retired to his palace at Split to grow cabbages.

journeys.name: Constantine's movements, 306-337
journeys.summary: Constantine's career can be drawn as a single line from the north-west corner of the empire to its eastern capital. Proclaimed by his father's army at York, he ruled Britain and Gaul from Trier for six years, fighting Franks on the Rhine and eliminating his father-in-law Maximian at Marseille. In 312 he crossed the Alps, took Turin and Verona and destroyed Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge under a sign he would later attribute to Christ. A first war with Licinius brought him the Balkans in 316-317; Serdica and Sirmium became his bases. The second war in 324 ended at Chrysopolis and made him sole emperor. He presided at Nicaea in 325, made a last and unhappy visit to Rome in 326, the year his son Crispus and wife Fausta died, and founded Constantinople. He died at a villa near Nicomedia in 337, baptised at the end.

journeys.name: Julian from Gaul to Persia, 355-363
journeys.summary: Julian was a 24-year-old student of philosophy when his cousin Constantius II made him Caesar and sent him to save Gaul from the Alamanni and Franks. He turned out to be a soldier. He relieved Cologne, survived a siege at Sens with a handful of men, and at Strasbourg in 357 routed seven Alamannic kings. He wintered at Paris, his 'dear Lutetia', and restored the Rhine. In February 360 his troops, ordered east, proclaimed him Augustus instead. Julian marched down the Danube in a fleet of river boats with astonishing speed; Constantius died in Cilicia before they met, and Julian entered Constantinople unopposed as sole emperor, already openly pagan. After a quarrelsome winter at Antioch he invaded Persia with perhaps 65,000 men, reached Ctesiphon, burned his fleet and was killed by a spear in a skirmish on the retreat.
journeys.note: After Ammianus 15-25 and Matthews, The Roman Empire of Ammianus (1989). The death site is placed by Ammianus near Maranga/Toummara; location approximate.

journeys.name: Egeria's pilgrimage, c. 381-384
journeys.summary: A single manuscript found at Arezzo in 1884 preserves part of a letter by a western woman, probably from Gallaecia in Spain, describing a three-year pilgrimage to the holy places to her 'sisters' at home. Egeria travelled with an escort, used the imperial post, and was received everywhere by bishops and monks who showed her the sites of the Bible. She climbed Sinai on a Sunday, saw the place of the burning bush, went to Mount Nebo to see what Moses saw, visited the tomb of Job, and travelled to Edessa to read the letter of Jesus to King Abgar in the original. Her account of the liturgy of Jerusalem, Holy Week, the veneration of the Cross and the Easter vigil, is the earliest detailed description of the Christian year. The surviving text breaks off at Constantinople, as she plans to visit Ephesus.

journeys.name: Jerome's wanderings, c. 360-420
journeys.summary: Born at Stridon on the Dalmatian-Pannonian border (its site is lost), Jerome studied grammar in Rome under Donatus and spent his student years, he later admitted, between the catacombs and the brothels. He tried the civil service at Trier, joined an ascetic circle at Aquileia, then set out for the East, where in a fever at Antioch he dreamed he was flogged before Christ's tribunal for being 'a Ciceronian, not a Christian'. He lived as a hermit in the desert of Chalcis, learning Hebrew from a converted Jew, was ordained at Antioch, studied with Gregory of Nazianzus at Constantinople, and became Pope Damasus' secretary in Rome, where he began revising the Latin Bible and gathered a circle of aristocratic women. Hounded out after Damasus' death, he settled at Bethlehem with Paula and spent 34 years translating the Hebrew Bible, the core of the Vulgate.

journeys.name: Augustine: Thagaste, Carthage, Rome, Milan, Hippo
journeys.summary: The Confessions turn Augustine's travels into a spiritual itinerary, and each city stands for a stage. Thagaste, a small Numidian town, was home, where his father Patricius scrimped to educate him and his mother Monica prayed. Carthage, 'a cauldron of illicit loves', gave him rhetoric, a concubine, a son and the Manichees. Rome in 383 disappointed: the students cheated on fees. Milan in 384, where he won the official chair of rhetoric through the pagan prefect Symmachus, gave him Ambrose's sermons, the Platonist books and the garden scene of 386 ('take up and read'). He was baptised by Ambrose at Easter 387. At Ostia, waiting for a ship home, he and Monica shared the vision of Confessions 9 days before she died. Back in Africa he founded a community at Thagaste, was press-ganged into the priesthood at Hippo in 391 and was its bishop for 34 years, dying as the Vandals besieged the city.

journeys.name: Melania the Younger, 408-439
journeys.summary: Melania was perhaps the richest woman in the Roman world, heiress of the Valerii with estates in Italy, Sicily, Africa, Spain and Britain yielding, her biographer claims, 120,000 pounds of gold a year. After losing two children she and her husband Pinianus took a vow of chastity and spent twenty years giving it all away, against the resistance of their families, the Senate and their own slaves, 8,000 of whom she freed. Alaric's approach drove them from Rome to Sicily and then Africa, where they founded monasteries at Thagaste with Augustine's friend Alypius; the congregation at Hippo tried to force Pinianus into the priesthood. In 417 they went to Jerusalem by way of the Egyptian desert. She founded monasteries on the Mount of Olives, visited Constantinople in 436-437 to convert her pagan uncle Volusianus, and returned to die in Jerusalem.

journeys.name: Galla Placidia: captive, queen and empress, 410-437
journeys.summary: The daughter of Theodosius I was in Rome when Alaric sacked it and became the Goths' most valuable hostage. She followed them south to Calabria, where Alaric died, and north into Gaul, and at Narbonne in January 414 she married Alaric's brother-in-law Athaulf in Roman dress, with the usurper Attalus singing the wedding song and 50 Gothic youths bringing gifts of looted gold. Their son, named Theodosius, died at Barcelona; Athaulf was murdered there in 415. Wallia traded her back to Ravenna for 600,000 measures of grain. Forced to marry the general Constantius, she became Augusta in 421, quarrelled with her brother Honorius and fled to Constantinople. When the usurper John was overthrown in 425 she returned as regent for her six-year-old son Valentinian III and governed the West for a dozen years.

journeys.name: Germanus of Auxerre to Britain, 429 (and Ravenna, 448)
journeys.summary: Germanus was a lawyer and provincial governor before he became bishop of Auxerre, and he brought both trades to Britain in 429. Prosper of Aquitaine says Pope Celestine sent him, at the deacon Palladius' prompting, to fight Pelagianism, which had taken hold among the British elite two decades after Roman rule ended. Constantius of Lyon's Life, written c. 480, is our only narrative: Germanus and Lupus of Troyes calmed a storm in the Channel, debated the Pelagians before a crowd at what was probably Verulamium, visited the shrine of St Alban, and then led a British force against a raiding party of Picts and Saxons, routing it without bloodshed by having the army shout 'Alleluia' three times in a mountain valley. It is one of the last glimpses of a functioning Romano-British society. Germanus died at Ravenna in 448 while pleading for the rebellious Armoricans at the court of Valentinian III.

journeys.name: Theodoric's march to Italy, 488-493
journeys.summary: Theodoric had grown up as a hostage in Constantinople and spent fifteen years as Zeno's most dangerous general, at one point camped outside the capital. Sending him west against Odoacer, 'to rule Italy until Zeno came', solved two problems at once. In autumn 488 the whole Ostrogothic people, perhaps 100,000 including women, children and wagons, left Novae on the Danube. They wintered on the road, fought their way past the Gepids at the river Ulca near Sirmium, crossed the Julian Alps in summer 489 and beat Odoacer at the Isonzo and Verona. Then came three years of war: defection by Odoacer's general Tufa, a Gothic defeat, the long siege of Ravenna. On 5 March 493 Odoacer surrendered on terms of shared rule; ten days later Theodoric killed him with his own hand at a banquet, saying 'there was not a bone in this wretch'.

journeys.name: Belisarius' voyage to Africa, 533
journeys.summary: Procopius sailed with the fleet as Belisarius' secretary, and his account of the voyage is a rare log of a Roman amphibious expedition: 500 transports, 92 dromons rowed by 2,000 marines, 30,000 sailors, 10,000 infantry and 5,000 cavalry. The patriarch blessed the flagship off the palace in June. At Abydos Belisarius impaled two drunken Hun allies who had killed a comrade; off Methone 500 men died from biscuit that the praetorian prefect John the Cappadocian had saved money on by half-baking it in the bath furnaces. After sixteen becalmed days in the Ionian Sea the fleet reached Sicily, where Procopius learned in Syracuse from a childhood friend's servant that the Vandal fleet was away in Sardinia. They landed unopposed at Caput Vada and marched up the coast, the fleet keeping pace offshore. Ten days later they were in Carthage.

journeys.name: Heraclius restores the True Cross, 629-630
journeys.summary: The Persians had carried the relic of the Cross from Jerusalem to Ctesiphon in 614, and recovering it became the emblem of Heraclius' war. After Khosrow II's fall, the general Shahrbaraz, master of the occupied Roman East, met Heraclius at Arabissos in July 629, agreed to evacuate Egypt and Syria in return for backing his own bid for the Persian throne, and handed over the relic. Heraclius went south through liberated Syria with his wife Martina, staying at Tiberias with a wealthy Jew, Benjamin, who converted, and on 21 March 630 he carried the Cross into Jerusalem on foot, the seals of its reliquary shown intact to the patriarch Modestus. It was the high point of the reign. Within six years Arab armies had taken the same road, and in 636 Heraclius sent the Cross to Constantinople for safety.
